page14_img_1.png.title: Summary box: participants' ratings of GPT-4 assumptions
page14_img_1.png.description: A gray rounded rectangular callout that highlights the study’s main summary statistics for GPT-4–generated assumptions: 86% of assumption ratings were judged partially or fully correct, 46% were rated relevant, and 31% were rated insightful. It also notes participants’ qualitative impressions that the generated assumptions were generally correct and comprehensive but showed a lack of software-engineering domain knowledge. These values summarize the paper’s RQ1 finding that GPT-4 can surface many correct assumptions yet often misses implicit, domain-specific insights.

page6_img_1.png.title: Workflow diagram of GPT-4 prompts for assumptions, analysis plans, and code
page6_img_1.png.description: A process diagram showing how seven empirical software engineering papers were fed into three GPT-4 prompt stages and corresponding evaluations. For RQ1 the papers produced 111 GPT-4-generated “Assumptions” via Prompt 1 (role: SE Researcher; info: methodology) which were returned as JSON and evaluated in a user study (red badge). For RQ2 the same papers produced 7 “Analysis Plans” via Prompt 2 (split methodology into JSON module specifications) that were also user‑study evaluated, and those modules yielded 23 code files via Prompt 3 (role/skills include MySQL and handling Git/GitHub data); the code (Python producing JSON outputs) was inspected in a code‑review workshop (blue badge). Arrows and icons indicate the linear pipeline: papers → prompts → model outputs (counts labeled) → human evaluation steps.

page7_img_2.png.title: Module specification: Data Extraction from Gousios commit comments
page7_img_2.png.description: A GPT-4–generated module card titled “Data Extraction” showing five labeled fields: Name, Description, Inputs, Outputs, and Methodology text. The description says the module extracts commit comments from the Gousios dataset—specifically comments from 90 top‑starred projects across the top programming languages on GitHub—and the methodology text reports a total of 60,425 commit comments analyzed. Inputs are listed as “None” and the output as “Extracted commit comments,” indicating this module is the pipeline’s initial data‑loading step and directly ties the generated specification back to the paper’s methodology.

page7_img_1.png.title: GPT-4 generated assumption: Confounding Factors in code review comments
page7_img_1.png.description: A screenshot of an example GPT‑4–generated assumption box titled “Confounding Factors” showing two fields: (1) Name and (2) Description. The description asserts that the primary confounders affecting how many comments a file receives are the number of lines added/deleted, whether the file is a test, and the number of commenters, and it explicitly acknowledges other potentially unconsidered factors such as change complexity, reviewer expertise, and code clarity. As an example from the study, this image illustrates how GPT‑4 converts methodology text into an explicit assumption by listing specific variables and noting possible omitted variables to consider in a replication.

page9_img_table_1.png.title: User study participant demographics and experience
page9_img_table_1.png.description: A tabular summary of the 14 study participants (IDs P1–P14) listing columns: number of publications, number of reviews, years of research, years of coding, frequency of LLM usage, location, gender, and job position. Values span a wide range (publications: 0–50; reviews: 0–20+; research experience: 1.5–15 years; coding experience: roughly 5–20 years, with one missing entry). LLM usage is reported as Daily, Weekly, or Yearly (many Daily users); locations are predominantly U.S. with two in India and one in Canada; genders are mixed. Reported positions vary from Ph.D. student and postdoc to senior and principal research/engineering managers, software engineer, and data scientist.

page10_img_table_1.png.title: Grading rubric for scoring assumptions, analysis plans, and modules
page10_img_table_1.png.description: A two-column table listing the evaluation constructs and the anchored rating descriptions used by study participants to score GPT-4 outputs. For Assumptions the table defines three constructs: correctness (1 = does not make the assumption, 2 = partially makes it, 3 = does make it), relevance (1–5 where 1 = does not need to be considered and 5 = must be considered for successful replication), and insightfulness (1–5 where 1 = does not reflect understanding and 5 = reflects deep understanding of SE methods/data). For Analysis plan correctness the 1–3 scale ranges from “cannot be used to repeat the study” to “can be used as‑is”; for Module-level ratings the correctness scale (1–3) ranges from “actions that should not be performed” to “actions that should be performed,” and descriptiveness (1–5) ranges from “unintelligible or too vague” to “clearly describes exact steps.” These anchored definitions were the standardized rubrics applied by the 14 expert participants in the user study to quantify GPT-4’s assumptions, plans, and module specifications.

page8_img_1.png.title: GPT-4–generated Python sentiment analysis using NLTK VADER
page8_img_1.png.description: A short Python snippet that GPT-4 produced to run sentiment analysis on a set of comments. The code imports json and NLTK, downloads the 'vader_lexicon', loads comments from './outputs/identification_of_security-related_comments_and_discussions.json', initializes SentimentIntensityAnalyzer, iterates over each comment calling sia.polarity_scores(comment) and appends {'comment': comment, 'sentiment': sentiment} to a results list. Finally it writes the aggregated results as pretty-printed JSON to './outputs/sentiment_analysis.json'; the sentiment object returned by polarity_scores is the per-comment score dictionary (e.g., neg/neu/pos/compound).

page12_img_1.png.title: Participant ratings of GPT-4-generated assumptions (correctness, relevance, insightfulness)
page12_img_1.png.description: Three side-by-side bar charts display how 367 participant ratings of GPT-4-generated assumptions are distributed across three dimensions. Correctness (1=Incorrect, 2=Partially correct, 3=Correct) is strongly skewed toward correct with counts 52, 89, and 226 respectively (86% rated partially or fully correct; μ≈2.5). Relevance (1–5) shows moderate ratings with counts 55, 76, 67, 86, and 83 (mean≈3.2), where ratings 4–5 make up about 46% of responses. Insightfulness (1–5) is weaker, with counts 64, 102, 88, 75, and 38 (mean≈2.8) and only about 31% of responses at the top insightfulness levels, indicating participants found the assumptions accurate and somewhat relevant but not especially insightful.

page4_img_table_1.png.title: Summary of selected papers with GPT‑4 generated assumptions and modules
page4_img_table_1.png.description: The table enumerates seven empirical software engineering papers and, for each, gives the citation key, publication venue, number of citations, a one-line description of the paper’s analysis, and counts of GPT-4–generated assumptions and analysis modules. From top to bottom the rows are: [36] ICSE’11 (94 citations) — API‑level refactorings and bug fixes — 18 assumptions, 4 modules; [57] ICSE’16 (85) — JavaScript performance issues — 17 assumptions, 4 modules; [17] MSR’11 (111) — bug‑fixing commits and changed lines — 15 assumptions, 4 modules; [27] MSR’14 (168) — sentiment in commit comments using SentiStrength — 14 assumptions, 2 modules; [51] MSR’14 (103) — sentiment in security‑related comments using nltk — 13 assumptions, 3 modules; [22] ESEC/FSE’22 (1) — pull‑request review comments and file position — 16 assumptions, 3 modules; [59] ICSE’22 (5) — commit‑message classification (what/why) — 18 assumptions, 3 modules. Overall, GPT‑4 produced between 13 and 18 assumptions and 2 to 4 modules per paper, while the papers span venues and citation counts from 1 up to 168.

page15_img_1.png.title: Participant ratings of analysis-plan and module correctness and descriptiveness
page15_img_1.png.description: Three adjacent bar charts summarize expert ratings of GPT-4’s analysis plans and modules. The left chart (Correctness — Plan) shows 3 ratings of 1 (Incorrect), 18 ratings of 2 (Partially correct), and 6 ratings of 3 (Correct) over N=27 plan ratings (paper reports μ=2.1/3 and 89% partially or fully correct). The middle chart (Correctness — Module) is labeled 55, 76, and 67 for ratings 1–3, indicating a plurality of partial-correct ratings at the module level (paper reports μ=2.4/3 and 72% partially or fully correct). The right chart (Descriptiveness — Module) gives a 1–5 distribution with most responses at 3 (32) and 4 (21) and fewer at the extremes (9 at 1, 12 at 5), aligning with the paper’s observation that module descriptions were only moderately descriptive (μ=3.2/5; ~38% rated descriptive).
